title: Cap. VI close: Maresius args VI–VIII — public person, Christ-parallel, covenant benefits
pass_a_gloss: Sixth, Maresius says Adam was a public person representing the whole human race more powerfully than the high priest represented Israel. Placeus says he can deny that as easily as Maresius affirms it; and even if granted, was some one first high-priestly act imputed to Israel? If yes, show Scripture; if no, how does this prove antecedent imputation of Adam's first actual sin alone? The high priest represented Israel by office as vessel of the legal covenant and bore them on shoulders and heart — is anything like that said of Adam? Seventh, Maresius says it is no less true that we sinned in Adam and so his sin is justly imputed to us all for punishment than that we, crucified with Christ, satisfied divine justice in him and so his satisfaction and obedience are imputed to us for righteousness. Placeus grants the first clause but says the dispute is only about the mode — antecedently/immediately, or through corruption? He affirms the latter; Maresius does not even try to prove the former, so he leaves the question-state between himself and Placeus. We are said to have satisfied in Christ as in our surety who satisfied in our place though he owed no satisfaction for himself — shall we say we sinned in Adam as in a surety who sinned in our place, as if we then owed obedience and Adam did not, and Adam stepped into our place to break the law for us? Placeus thinks Maresius would not like that. And Christ's satisfaction is imputed through our consent or faith, so the parallel at most yields Adam's sin imputed through our consent habitually wrapped in hereditary vice — which is Placeus's own view. Eighth and last: Maresius says imputation of Adam's sin is fairer because as Adam received life's condition and promise not for himself only but for posterity if he stood, so by his fall he should contract death's guilt not for himself only but for all his — benefits and burdens travel together. Placeus asks how that is meant. If it means posterity would have lived under the same life-condition and promise — perpetual life if they did not break God's law — that is most true, for children share their fathers' covenant. If it means Adam would have communicated preserved original righteousness to posterity — also most true, but what is that to antecedent imputation of Adam's sin? By sinning he stripped himself of original righteousness, contracted corruption, propagated that privation and corruption, and through it his death-guilt; so being under sin's and death's law he begot children under the same, communicating his sin and through sin death. If it means Adam's righteousness, had he stood, would have been imputed to all posterity for eternal life — Garissoles denies and refutes that; whence can it be known?; and Adam would have needed to beget children unlike himself, immutable or impeccable, else they would be at once just by paternal imputation and unjust by their own sin, worthy of life and death together. If you say they would fall from that imputation by sinning, then the imputation was superfluous — useless if they sinned, and no more needed than Adam's own righteousness when they were righteous by their own. So the argument overturns rather than establishes antecedent imputation. Who believes the most equal God set Adam a law such that constant perpetual obedience would not be imputed to posterity, yet a single act of disobedience would be — so that as to imputation obedience and disobedience would stand in contrary ways?
pass_b_english: VI. But I do not know what proof he subjoins. For he was a public person, and represented the whole human race far more effectually than the high Priest in the sanctuary represented the whole Israelite nation. First, cannot that be denied by me as easily as it is affirmed by the learned man? Next, grant it is so — was therefore some one, and that the first, action of the high Priest imputed to the Israelite nation? If you say yes, give a place of Scripture that teaches it. If you deny, what does this do toward proving the imputation of Adam's first actual sin alone, and that antecedent? The high priest represented the Israelite people by office, as vessel of the legal covenant, and in a manner bore him upon shoulders and heart. Is anything of that kind said of Adam? VII. Nor is it less true, he says, that we have sinned in Adam, and so his sin is justly imputed to us all for punishment, than that afterward we, crucified together with Christ, have satisfied divine justice in him, and so his satisfaction and obedience are deservedly imputed to us before God for righteousness. I confess that we have sinned in Adam, and that his sin is justly imputed to us all for punishment. But that is not now in question between us. The question is only about the mode of imputation, or, so to speak, the species: whether it is imputed antecedently or immediately, or through corruption? This I affirm; that the distinguished man does not even try to prove. He therefore wanders from the state of the question which ought to have been between him and Placeus. For the rest, we are said to have satisfied divine justice in Christ as in our surety, who satisfied in our place, when he ought in no way to satisfy for himself. Shall we say likewise that we have sinned in Adam as in our surety, who would have sinned in our place? To be sure, we were then bound to obey God, Adam not likewise. And he came into our place, that he might violate the law in our place. Does this please the most celebrated man? I do not think so. And I have already observed that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us through our consent or faith: and so nothing can be made of that comparison, except at most that Adam's sin is imputed to us through our consent, which is habitually included in hereditary vice: which is Placeus's very own judgment. VIII. In the last place he fights with this argument. And this imputation of Adam's sin is so much the fairer, because as he had received the condition and promise of life not for himself only but also for his posterity if he stood, so he ought by his fall to have contracted the guilt of death not for himself only but also for all his: for it is most equal that to whom the advantages belong, to him the burdens and disadvantages also belong. How does he understand that Adam had received the condition and promise of life not for himself only but also for his posterity if he stood? Thus — that Adam's posterity would have been under the same condition and promise of life under which Adam was, that is, would live forever if they had not violated God's law? This is most true. For under whatever covenant the fathers are, under the same their children also are. Or that Adam would have communicated to posterity his original righteousness which he had preserved? Nothing truer; but what is that to the imputation of Adam's sin, especially antecedent? By his sin he deprived himself of original righteousness, and contracted corruption, and propagated that privation and corruption into posterity, and through it his own guilt of death. So, as he was under the law of sin and death, so he begot children likewise under the law of sin and death. For he communicated to them his sin, and through sin death. Or finally does he understand that Adam's righteousness, if he had stood, would have been imputed to all his posterity for eternal life? First D. Garissoles denies this, and refutes it with several arguments, in the book on the Imputation of the first sin, chapter 15, section 14, pages 510–511. Next, whence can that be known? Finally, Adam would have had to beget children unlike himself, that is, immutable or impeccable. For let us suppose they sinned: they would have been at once both righteous by imputation of paternal righteousness and unrighteous by their own sin, and so at once worthy of both life and death. If you say they would have fallen from that imputation by sinning, I shall reply that that imputation would therefore have been superfluous and useless, inasmuch as, if they had sinned, it would have been of no use to them; seeing they would have been no less righteous by their own righteousness than Adam himself had been. This argument therefore avails rather to overturn than to establish the antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. For who would believe that the most equal God set Adam such a law, that if he obeyed, however constantly and perpetually, his obedience would not be imputed to posterity, yet his disobedience would be imputed if he happened even once not to obey; and so (as far as imputation is concerned) obedience and disobedience would stand in a contrary way?

VI. Sed nescio quid subiicit probationis. Erat quippe is persona publica et totum genus humanum repraesentabat longe efficacius quam summus Sacerdos in sanctuario totam gentem Israeliticam. Primum, nonne id aeque facile negari a me potest, ac affirmatur a viro docto? Deinde, fac ita esse, an igitur una aliqua, eaque prima, summi Sacerdotis actio genti Israeliticae imputabatur? Si ais, da locum Scripturae qui id doceat. Si negas, quid hoc facit ad probandam imputationem solius primi peccati actualis Adami, et quidem antecedentem? Repraesentabat populum Israeliticum summus sacerdos ex munere, ut vas foederis legalis, eumque super humeris et corde, quodammodo gestabat. Diciturne tale quid de Adamo?

VII. Nec minus, inquit, verum est, nos in Adamo peccasse, adeoque iuste nobis omnibus eius peccatum ad poenam imputari, quam postea nos concrucifixos Christo in ipso satisfecisse iustitiae divinae, adeoque merito eius satisfactionem et obedientiam nobis imputari apud Deum ad iustitiam. Fateor nos in Adamo peccasse, et iuste nobis omnibus eius peccatum ad poenam imputari. Sed id nunc quidem inter nos non versatur in quaestione. Quaeritur tantum de imputationis modo, seu, ut ita loquar, specie: utrum antecedenter seu immediate imputetur, an mediante corruptione? Hoc affirmo, illud vir Clar. probare, nec conatur quidem. Aberrat igitur a statu quaestionis, quae inter ipsum et Placeum esse debebat. Ceterum in Christo satisfecisse iustitiae divinae dicimur, tanquam in vade nostro, qui loco nostro satisfecit, cum is pro se satisfacere nullo modo deberet. Dicemurne similiter peccasse nos in Adamo tanquam in vade nostro, qui loco nostro peccasset? Scilicet nos tunc tenebamur Deo parere, Adamus non item. Ille autem in locum nostrum venit, ut nostro loco legem violaret. Hoccine placet viro celeberrimo? non arbitror. Iam autem observavi satisfactionem Christi nobis imputari mediante consensu nostro seu fide: itaque nihil ex illa comparatione effici posse, nisi ad summum peccatum Adami nobis imputari mediante consensu nostro, qui habitualiter in vitio haereditario includitur: quae ipsissima Placei sententia est.

VIII. Ultimo loco hoc pugnat argumento. Atque haec peccati Adamici imputatio eo aequior est, quod sicut vitae conditionem et promissionem non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis posteris acceperat, si staret, ita debuit mortis reatum suo lapsu non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis omnibus contraxisse: nam ad quem pertinent commoda, ad eum quoque onera et incommoda pertinere aequissimum est. Quomodo intelligit Adamum vitae conditionem et promissionem non sibi tantum sed etiam suis posteris accepisse si staret? An sic, posteros Adami futuros fuisse sub eadem conditione et promissione vitae, sub qua erat Adamus, hoc est, perpetuo victuros, si Dei legem non violassent? Hoc verissimum est. Nam sub quo foedere sunt patres, sub eodem etiam eorum liberi sunt. An Adamum communicaturum cum posteris iustitiam suam originalem, quam conservasset, fuisse? Nihil verius, sed quid ista ad imputationem peccati Adamici, praesertim antecedentem? Peccato suo se privavit iustitia originali, et corruptionem contraxit, eamque privationem et corruptionem propagavit in posteros, et per eam suum mortis reatum. Quare, ut fuit sub lege peccati et mortis, sic liberos genuit similiter sub lege peccati et mortis. Communicavit enim cum illis suum peccatum, et per peccatum mortem. An denique intelligit, iustitiam Adami, si stetisset, omnibus eius posteris ad vitam aeternam imputandam fuisse? Primum hoc negat, et aliquot argumentis refellit D. Garissolius lib. de Imput. primi peccati cap. xv. §. 14. pag. 510. 511. Deinde, unde id sciri potest? Denique, oportuisset Adamum gignere liberos sibi dissimiles, hoc est, immutabiles seu impeccabiles. Ponamus enim eos peccasse, fuissent simul et iusti imputatione paternae iustitiae, et iniusti proprio peccato, atque adeo simul et vita et morte digni. Si dixeris, peccando ab illa imputatione excidisse, reponam igitur illam imputationem superfluam ac inutilem fuisse, quippe quae, si peccassent, eis nullo fuisset usui; utpote non minus propria iustitia iustis, quam ipse fuerat Adamus. Valet igitur hoc argumentum ad evertendam potius quam ad stabiliendam imputationem antecedentem Adamici peccati. Quis enim credat, Deum aequissimum eam legem posuisse Adamo, ut si obediret, quantumvis constanter et perpetuo, non imputaretur eius obedientia posteris, imputaretur tamen eius inobedientia, si contingeret eum vel semel non obedire; atque ita (quod ad imputationem attinet) contrario modo sese obedientia et inobedientia haberent?

choices.point: Close Cap. VI on arg. VIII
choices.decision: §22 ends Maresius series before Cap. VII
